name: George Cecil Ives
bio: Poet, penologist and pioneering campaigner for homosexual law reform; illegitimate son of Colonel Gordon Maynard Gordon-Ives and, by his own account, the Baroness de Molarti of Spain, raised by his paternal grandmother and living on a private income. Kept a diary from 1886 to 1950 - 122 volumes, around three million words - alongside a forty-five-volume press-cuttings casebook, an archive now split between Yale and the University of Texas at Austin. In about 1893 he founded the Order of Chaeronea, the first homosexual support-and-pressure group in Britain, named for the Theban band slaughtered in 338 BC, and structured it deliberately without hierarchy: any two existing members could invite a third. In October 1894 he published an outspoken justification of same-sex love in the Humanitarian. Lived at 56 St James' Street from July 1891, at Flat E4 the Albany, Piccadilly, from 30 June 1894, from 1897 in his late grandmother's Regent's Park house, and from 1905 at Adelaide Road, Primrose Hill, with an unconventional household of younger working-class men he called his 'children' - a family connected by co-residence rather than by blood. He was treasurer of the British Society for the Study of Sex Psychology (Edward Carpenter was its life president). Though he identified settledly as homosexual, he also had affairs with women, and considered having a child outside marriage with Matilda 'Tilly' Hayes. His will of 1939, eight typed pages with ten later codicils, left the Adelaide Road house and contents to the two men he was then living with, Harold Bloodworth and Stanley Saunders.
bio_note: Born/died and Order founding from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 573 n. 3: 'George Cecil Ives (1867-1950). Albany move-in date from p. 592 n. 3. Parentage, diary scope (1886-1950, 122 vols, c. 3M words), casebook, archive split, Chaeronea-as-first-group, Humanitarian article, and addresses from Cook (2003) pp. 31, 143-8. Cook spells the Order 'Chaerona'. Lewis (NHC podcast) notes the Spanish-baroness maternal descent is not borne out by census records. Enriched from Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), ch. 'George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family': the Regent's Park interval (from 1897), the Order's non-hierarchical two-members-invite-a-third structure, the BSSSP treasurership with Carpenter as life president, the affairs with women and the Tilly Hayes child question, and the 1939 will. Pagination: printed folio = PDF page - 11 in the body text, - 10 in the back-matter notes. The Ives chapter runs printed 95-111, not 95-123; ch. 5 (Joe Ackerley) begins at printed 112, and the 'Freddie' of printed 113 onward is Ackerley's lover, a different man from the household's Freddie Smith. Cook 2014 spells the Order 'the Order of the Chaeronea' (Cook 2003 has 'Chaerona'). Cook dates the Albany move to 1893 ('two years later' than 1891) against the Complete Letters' 30 June 1894, and dates the will to October 1939 in his text but 1 December 1939 in his endnote 80 - both unresolved. Provenance caveat: Cook's endnotes credit Brian Lewis, by personal communication and with no archival citation, for the Goddard-daughters departure reading (n. 22), the Tilly Hayes identification (n. 61), and the Charles French connection (n. 84).

context_engagements.period: Adelaide Road household, from 1905; departure undated
context_engagements.note: He left to move in with Robert 'Robbie' Ross, whom Cook describes as a good friend of both Ives and Wilde. Strong caveat: this single sentence is the only mention of Freddie Smith in the whole 336-page book, and Cook cites nothing for it - the attached endnote 21 is purely methodological (Gilding, Behlmer, McBride and McCandless, Tosh, on household and family).

sources.quote: Also in the house were Pug and Elephant and other intimate male friends of Ives who became housemates for often extended periods before moving on - often to marry, or in the case of Freddie Smith to move in with Robbie Ross who was a good friend of both Ives and Wilde.
sources.context: Cook, on the turnover of the Adelaide Road household
sources.supports: Freddie Smith's household membership and his departure to live with Robert Ross - the Ives-circle/Wilde-circle bridge.

context_engagements.note: A woman with whom Cook says Ives had a long-running 'affair/friendship' across three decades, and with whom he discussed having a child - the 'certain girl' of the 1920 diary entry. She stood third in line to inherit the Adelaide Road house under his 1939 will, after Bloodworth and Saunders and ahead of his kin, and Cook names her among the friendships Ives kept up 'close and open'. Cook's compound 'affair/friendship' is deliberately unresolved and should be preserved rather than collapsed to either term. Caveat: Cook's endnote 61 credits the identification of Hayes with the 'certain girl' to Brian Lewis by personal communication, with no archival citation.

sources.quote: This was Matilda (Tilly) Hayes with whom Ives had a long running affair/friendship from the 1910s to the 1940s.
sources.context: Cook, identifying the 'certain girl' with whom Ives had discussed having children in a 1920 diary entry
sources.supports: A named, decades-long relationship with a woman, in Cook's own deliberately unresolved formulation.

sources.quote: she attracted me physically (not the romantic love; no girl can win that from me) [.] she said she wanted a baby but only under married conditions.
sources.context: Ives's diary (vol. 76, 14 September 1920, p. 20, per Cook's endnote 62), quoted by Cook as a displayed block quotation; the ellipsis is Cook's own
sources.supports: Ives's own account of the relationship: physical attraction, romantic love explicitly withheld, marriage refused.
sources.speaker: George Ives, diary

context_engagements.period: Named in the 1939 will; bequest later revoked
context_engagements.note: Cook reads him as probably working-class and service-sector, and suggests he was 'perhaps a former lover' - but immediately offers the competing reading that French was one of the men Ives called 'Ducks', short for 'lame ducks', men he helped out intermittently but thought hopeless cases. Any certainty must not exceed Cook's own hedge, which is explicitly speculative; and his endnote 84 credits the connection to Brian Lewis by personal communication, with no archival citation.

sources.quote: Probably working-class, employed in the service sector (which we've already seen had a reputation for attracting queer men), French was perhaps a former lover, though was also one of the men Ives went on to call 'Ducks' (short for 'lame ducks' - men he helped out intermittently but thought hopeless cases).
sources.context: Cook, on a legatee named in Ives's 1939 will as having worked at the Spread Eagle Hotel, Midhurst, and latterly at 1 Greek Street, London W1
sources.supports: Charles French as a possible former lover of Ives - Cook's own speculation, offered alongside a competing non-sexual reading.

context_engagements.note: Poet, and named by Cook as a fellow member of the Order of Chaeronea. Not a partner; an Order-kinship tie, which is the relation Cook argues Ives understood as a form of family. This is a firmer Order-membership attestation than Cook's hedged sentence about Radclyffe Hall and Una, Lady Troubridge (printed 108), who 'seem to have been considered'.

sources.quote: He left the poet and fellow member of the Order of the Chaeronea, Laurence Housman, a ring bearing the numbers 338 (the date of the last battle of the Theban Bands).
sources.context: Cook, on the bequests in Ives's 1939 will beyond his kin and household
sources.supports: Housman's membership of the Order of Chaeronea alongside Ives, and a personal bequest marking it.
